notes.h: Why fruit and vegetables are commercially processed
notes.b: Fresh fruit and vegetables spoil quickly, so manufacturers process them, often close to the farm soon after harvest. Processing turns a perishable crop into a product that lasts and is easy to use.
points: Processing changes fresh produce into products with a longer shelf life, greater convenience, availability all year and less waste, or a mixture of these.
The three main commercial methods for fruit and vegetables are freezing, canning and drying (also called dehydration).

Steps common to the methods are sorting, washing, peeling, cutting, blanching or cooking (blanching is a short dip in boiling water or steam), packaging and labelling. Brine, syrup, juice or additives may also be added.

Spoilage is caused by enzymes (natural chemicals in the food that make it deteriorate) and micro-organisms such as bacteria and moulds. Every preservation method works by inactivating, killing or preventing the activity of one or both.

Processed products must be labelled under Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011 on food information to consumers, which applies in Ireland through the European Union (Provision of Food Information to Consumers) Regulations 2014.
notes.tip: Short items ask you to match or name the methods, for example that dehydration removes moisture. Learn the three methods and what each does to the enzymes and micro-organisms.

notes.b: Freezing keeps food by cold rather than heat, so the fresh colour and flavour are largely kept. The way the food is frozen decides whether its texture survives.
points: Process: the fruit or vegetables are washed and prepared, vegetables are blanched, then they are frozen quickly and packed in moisture-proof packaging. They are stored and distributed at -18 degrees Celsius or lower.

Principle: low temperature stops micro-organisms multiplying and slows enzymes, and the water in the food becomes ice, which micro-organisms cannot use. Freezing does not kill them, it only stops their growth and activity.
Vegetables are blanched before freezing to destroy the enzymes that would otherwise keep working and cause deterioration. Blanching does not sterilise the food and does not kill all micro-organisms.
Quick freezing at about -25 degrees Celsius forms small ice crystals, which damage the cell walls very little, so the food keeps its texture.
Slow freezing forms large ice crystals that rupture the cell walls, so the food becomes limp and loses juice (called drip) on thawing.
Air blast freezing blows very cold air through a tunnel over food carried on a conveyor belt.
Plate (contact) freezing presses the food between two cold metal plates, which suits flat items.
Flow (fluidised bed) freezing blows cold air up through a perforated belt so that each piece freezes separately and does not stick together. It suits peas.
Cryogenic freezing immerses or sprays food with liquid nitrogen and suits delicate foods such as strawberries.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the two temperatures: -25 degrees Celsius is the quick freezing temperature that gives small crystals, and -18 degrees Celsius is the storage temperature. Give a suitable food for each commercial method (peas for flow freezing).

notes.h: Effects of freezing on nutrients and quality
notes.b: Frozen vegetables keep most of their goodness, but a few vitamins are lost along the way. Knowing where they go is a favourite exam point.
points: Vitamin C and B vitamins are lost into the blanching water and into the drip on thawing, so thaw as little as possible and cook vegetables from frozen.
Colour, flavour and most nutrients are well retained when freezing is carried out properly. Frozen produce can contain more vitamin C than 'fresh' produce stored for several days.
Foods with a high water content and delicate texture, such as lettuce and bananas, do not freeze well because they go soft and mushy on thawing.
Frozen foods are convenient, with little waste and no salt added.
notes.tip: If asked how vitamins B1 and C are lost when freezing vegetables, name the blanching water, the drip from slow freezing and thawing before cooking. True/false items test lettuce and bananas, and blanching before freezing.

notes.b: Canning keeps food by heat. The food is sealed in a container and sterilised, so it keeps for a long time with no fridge, but the heat costs some nutrients and texture.
points: Process: produce is washed, graded, peeled and cut, then blanched or cooked briefly. It is packed into cans or jars with brine, syrup, juice or water, sealed with the air removed, heated in a retort (an industrial pressure cooker heated above boiling point) to sterilise it, then cooled.
Heat sterilisation destroys micro-organisms and enzymes, and the airtight seal stops them re-entering. Canned food therefore has a long shelf life without refrigeration until opened.
Canning causes loss of water-soluble vitamins (vitamin C, thiamine and folate) through the heat and by leaching (dissolving out) into the liquid, so the liquid should be used.
Canning changes the colour, texture and flavour of fruit and vegetables, which become softer and duller.
Canned vegetables contain added salt in the brine, which raises their sodium content. Vegetables in water or with no added salt are lower in sodium.
Syrup raises the sugar content of canned fruit. People controlling their blood glucose should choose fruit in natural juice or water, which has less added sugar.
Fibre, minerals, carotene and protein are well kept in canned foods.
Advantages: long shelf life, ready to use, cheap, available all year, and safe from spoilage if the can is undamaged.
Disadvantages: added salt or sugar, loss of vitamin C and thiamine, and altered texture.
notes.tip: In 'explain the effect of canning' questions, give vitamin losses, changes in colour, texture and flavour, destruction of micro-organisms and enzymes, and added sugar, salt or fat from the liquid. Say canning is heat sterilisation, unlike freezing and drying. When a table compares fresh, frozen and canned peas, state the data, then give a reason: sodium rises because of brine, and vitamin C and thiamine fall because of high temperature and long processing.

notes.b: Drying keeps food by taking its water away. Without water, spoilage cannot happen, so dried foods are light, compact and cheap to store and transport.
points: Process: the produce is washed, cut and usually blanched or treated with a preservative. Most of the water is removed by controlled warm air (hot-air drying), or by sun drying, spray drying or freeze-drying. It is then sealed in moisture-proof packaging.
Removing water leaves none available to micro-organisms and enzymes, so micro-organisms cannot grow and enzymes cannot work. Dried food keeps for months without refrigeration.
Dehydration may reduce B vitamins, vitamin A and vitamin E, and it alters colour, texture and flavour. The food shrinks and becomes chewy.
Vitamin C is lost unless a sulphite preservative is used.
Dried fruit such as raisins, sultanas, apricots and prunes is concentrated in sugar, energy and fibre because most of the water has been removed.
Dried peas, beans and lentils are pulses that keep for long periods and are rehydrated (soaked or cooked) before use.
Other examples are instant mashed potato and dried herbs.
notes.tip: For 'explain the effect of dehydration', give the vitamin losses, changes to colour, texture and flavour, the control of micro-organisms and enzymes by removing water, and the concentrated sugar in dried fruit.

notes.h: Additives in processed fruit and vegetables
notes.b: Processing can spoil the colour of produce, let it brown or take out nutrients. Additives are substances added to food to put these right and to help it keep.
points: Additives improve colour, flavour, texture and keeping quality, replace nutrients lost in processing, and make processing and storage easier. Approved additives are identified by E numbers.
Food additives are approved under Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 on food additives, and the label must list them by function and name or number.
Colourings, in the E100 to E180 range, restore or enhance colour lost during processing, for example in canned peas and other canned vegetables.
Preservatives prevent micro-organisms from growing. Sulphur dioxide (E220) is used as a preservative in some dried fruit, and sugar and salt also act as preservatives.
Antioxidants prevent browning. Ascorbic acid, which is vitamin C (E300), is used to stop cut or frozen fruit darkening.
Flavourings, sweeteners, acids, firming agents and bulking agents are added to some canned and processed fruit and vegetables, and must be declared on the label.
Nutrient fortification (adding nutrients) improves nutritive value where nutrients are lost in processing.
notes.tip: If asked to name two additives used in processed fruit or vegetables, give a colouring in canned vegetables, a preservative or an antioxidant. Then say why additives are used: to improve colour, flavour, texture and keeping qualities, and to replace nutrients lost in processing.

notes.b: Processed fruit and vegetables save time and effort, but what is added or taken out during processing changes their nutritional value.
points: Examples: frozen peas and mixed vegetables, canned beans, tomatoes and sweetcorn, dried fruit, bagged salad and stir-fry mixes, fruit juices, smoothies, fruit salads in juice, fruit yoghurts, jam, vegetable soups, ready meals and sauces with vegetables, and potato products (chips, wedges, crisps, instant mash).
Advantages: they save time, skill and effort, are available all year, have a long shelf life, cause little waste and can be fortified. Some, such as frozen vegetables, retain nutrients well.

Disadvantages: they are often higher in salt, sugar and fat than fresh produce and lower in fibre and vitamins. They are also more expensive, create packaging waste, have lower sensory quality, and can unbalance the diet if eaten too often.
Vegetable crisps and wedges are high in fat and salt, so they are better counted as snacks than as a serving of vegetables.
Vegetables in soups, sauces and ready meals often contain added salt, fat and sugar, which lowers their nutritional value compared with fresh vegetables.

Fruit juice, whether fresh natural juice or made from concentrate, has the sugars of the fruit with little fibre. Juice and smoothies therefore lack the fibre of whole fruit and are not a full replacement for it.
Unsweetened juice counts as at most one serving a day. Check labels for added sugar.

Processed products must carry an ingredients list (in descending order of weight), additives with their functions, net quantity, a date mark (best before or use by), storage instructions, cooking instructions where needed, and nutritional information (energy, fat, saturates, carbohydrate, sugars, protein, salt).

Allergens must be shown in bold or otherwise emphasised in the ingredients list. The law is Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, in force in Ireland through the European Union (Provision of Food Information to Consumers) Regulations 2014.
notes.tip: Advantages and disadvantages of convenience and processed foods (tinned, packet) are examined, so prepare both lists. Remember that frozen vegetables are not less nutritious than fresh, because fresh produce stored for several days can lose as much vitamin C.

keyTerms.definition: Brief immersion of vegetables in boiling water followed by rapid cooling, used before freezing to denature enzymes.
Heating sealed food to a temperature that destroys micro-organisms and enzymes, allowing long storage without refrigeration.
A solution of salt in water used as a packing liquid for canned vegetables.
The removal of water from food by drying, which prevents the growth of micro-organisms and the action of enzymes.
The juice released from frozen food on thawing, which carries away water-soluble vitamins and minerals.
A code that identifies an approved food additive in the EU, such as E100 for a colouring or E300 for ascorbic acid.
A food that has been partly or fully prepared, so that less time is needed to make it ready to eat.
A juice from which most of the water has been removed, which is reconstituted with water before sale.

questions.prompt: Outline two ways in which canning changes the nutritional value of vegetables.
questions.model: Any two: water-soluble vitamins such as vitamin C are lost into the liquid and through heat; the brine adds salt, so the sodium content rises; some fibre and minerals are lost into the packing liquid.

questions.prompt: Compare freezing, canning and drying as methods of processing vegetables, referring to nutritive value, texture, flavour and shelf life, and describe how additives are used in processed fruit and vegetables.
questions.model: Freezing: blanching denatures enzymes; slow freezing forms large ice crystals that damage cell walls and cause drip loss; some vitamin C and B vitamins are lost in blanching water and drip; colour and flavour are well retained; long shelf life in a freezer. Canning: heat sterilisation destroys micro-organisms and enzymes, giving a long shelf life without refrigeration; water-soluble vitamins are lost, colour, texture and flavour change, and sodium rises from brine. Drying: removing water prevents micro-organisms and enzyme activity; dried fruit is concentrated in sugar and energy and fibre; B vitamins, vitamin A and vitamin E may be reduced; texture and flavour change. Additives: colourings in the E100 to E180 range restore colour, preservatives such as sulphur dioxide (E220) prevent spoilage, antioxidants such as ascorbic acid (E300) prevent browning, and flavourings and sweeteners are added and declared on the label; additives are approved under Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008.
